extracted.intended_audience: educated general public, scientists, philosophers, educators, parents, and physicians interested in logic of science and mental/educational practice
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for conducting and judging inductive (synthetic) reasoning and for evaluating nervous/mental activity and educational practices; includes sampling rules, probabilistic justification of induction, presumptions for evaluating theories, and five-point classification of brain activity for guiding education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive (synthetic) reasoning is a process of sampling: a number of specimens of a class are taken (at random) and used to infer properties of the whole class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specimens must be taken at random from the class of interest; agreement in a sample can support an induction only when sampling procedures are appropriate. Treat a sample as representing the class only when random selection and representativeness are satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predesignation of the character (predesignated/predetermined)
rubrics_metrics.description: An induction has full force when the character to be examined is designated before taking the sample; if the character is not previously designated, a prevalent character in a sample only suggests possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the character beforehand for its importance, obviousness, or other interest; if a character is observed post hoc, draw a second independent sample to test whether it is actually prevalent rather than an accidental agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative/random sampling (avoid selecting sub-classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliable synthetic conclusions require that the specimens by which we judge have been taken at random from the class about which we infer, and not selected as belonging to any sub-class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check sampling methodology to ensure it is not biased toward a sub-class; only random (or appropriately randomized) samples justify strong inductive inferences about the larger class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of simultaneous inductive inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same sample to make multiple independent inductive inferences reduces the certainty that all inferences are correct compared with making each separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when inferring multiple characters from a single sample; the probability that all inferences hold falls as the number of simultaneous inferences increases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportionate/statistical induction requires probabilistic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Inferences about proportions (e.g., about the fraction of a population with some trait) are not adequately explained by treating the sample as a single instance; they require probabilistic analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not reduce proportionate induction to single-instance induction; use probability theory and statistical reasoning to assess the strength of proportion-based conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity of Nature is not a sufficient warrant for induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine that induction depends solely on the uniformity of Nature overlooks essential conditions (like random sampling and predesignation) that are necessary for valid induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid attributing inductive validity only to general uniformity; explicitly verify sampling principles and the relevance/constancy of the character in question rather than relying on a vague appeal to uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance/obviousness of characters (practical selection of what to examine)
rubrics_metrics.description: We typically examine characters that have importance, interest, or obviousness to us; treating these as predetermined (practically equivalent to predesignation) justifies inferring that the sample represents the class in these respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus sampling and analysis on characters that matter for the question at hand; recognize that choosing salient characters reduces the risk of spurious, accidental patterns dominating the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-hoc findings require confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: A character discovered to be prevalent in a sample but not preselected can only suggest that it may be prevalent in the whole class and must be tested with further sampling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat post-hoc discoveries as hypotheses to be tested by additional independent samples rather than as established inductive conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every empirical rule may have exceptions; avoid assuming absolute universality
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an easy corollary that every empirical rule has an exception; we have no right to assume any induction is absolutely without exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain epistemic humility: avoid categorical conclusions of universality from empirical induction; seek explanatory mechanisms and beware overgeneralization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek causal subclasses that explain statistical regularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a statistical induction (e.g., roughly half births are male), it is usually possible, by prolonged investigation, to discover a class for which the predicate holds universally (i.e., find the causal conditions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use statistical patterns as guides to search for more specific classes or causes; discovery requires directed inquiry (a 'scent') and is unlikely without appropriate guiding hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probability doctrine to justify and systematize induction
rubrics_metrics.description: The explanation of induction by the doctrine of probabilities is not a mere metaphysical formula but one from which all rules of synthetic reasoning can be deduced systematically and with mathematical cogency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground inductive practice in probabilistic reasoning; derive rules of sampling, inference, and confidence from probability theory rather than ad hoc principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption in favor of mechanical/explainable theories
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone claims to have discovered a plan, scheme, regularity, or correspondence (e.g., in classification, development, or human affairs), the first question is whether such relations are susceptible of explanation on mechanical principles; if not, they should be viewed with disfavour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate new theoretical claims by asking whether mechanical (naturalistic, causal) explanations are possible; prefer hypotheses continuous with known experience and mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against mystical theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific minds ought to have a strong presumption against mystical theories—those that have no possibility of being mechanically explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mystical explanations skeptically; require strong, unusual evidence before accepting theories that posit non-mechanical causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that unknown parts of space/time resemble known parts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of evidence to the contrary, the unknown parts of space and time should be presumed to be like the known parts (occupied, subject to similar cycles), rather than invoking radically different conceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer continuity with observed phenomena when extrapolating to unobserved regions; avoid ad hoc hypotheses that posit fundamentally different kinds of entities or events without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inferring global design from limited evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the universe is infinite or without a definable whole, attempts to find a design embracing the whole are futile; claims that Nature's arrangements are benevolent, just, or wise should be met with prejudice because of the presumption of vastness and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of broad teleological claims based on limited local evidence; require strong justification before attributing moral or teleological properties to Nature as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nervous/mental activity: Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: One of five points of view for regarding nervous activities is their Quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When directing cultivation of mental function, consider the qualitative aspects (e.g., kind or character of mental states) alongside other dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nervous/mental activity: Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider nervous activities in terms of their Quantity as a distinct aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the amount or intensity of mental activity (e.g., volume of cognitive work) when planning education or evaluating brain health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nervous/mental activity: Tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the Tension of nervous activities as a separate point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the level of nervous/mental tension or strain (e.g., sustained effort, stress) and manage it in pedagogy and health interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nervous/mental activity: Variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety is a distinct aspect for regarding nervous activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In educational design and brain cultivation, ensure adequate variety in activities to promote balanced development and avoid monotony-induced harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nervous/mental activity: Control
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of nervous activities is the fifth listed point of view for classifying mental function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess and cultivate control (volitional regulation, attention control, executive function) as part of mental development and brain-strengthening practices.
